::: {.flashcard-page}

This confused me a lot when I started learning Rust. “Colon colon angle
bracket” is what I searched for first because I had no idea the syntax had a
name. It does: **turbofish**.

::: {.flashcard-stage}
::: {.flashcard-card}
<div class="flashcard-meta">
  <span class="flashcard-number">Flashcard 05</span>
  <span class="flashcard-topic">Rust</span>
</div>

<div class="flashcard-eyebrow">The question</div>

::: {#flashcard-question .flashcard-question role="heading" aria-level="2"}
What does `::<T>` tell the Rust compiler?
:::

<p class="flashcard-hint">Think about what <code>parse</code> knows before the result has a concrete type.</p>

<details class="flashcard-reveal">
  <summary>Reveal the answer</summary>
<div class="flashcard-answer"><p>It supplies a concrete generic type when Rust cannot infer one from the surrounding code.</p></div>
</details>
:::
:::

## Where I hit it

I had a string containing pi and wanted to parse it into a number:

```rust
fn main() {
    let pi_string = "3.1415";
    let pi_float = pi_string.parse().unwrap();
    println!("{}", pi_float);
}
```

It looks reasonable, but `parse` can produce many different types. At this
point Rust has no way to know whether I want an `f32`, an `f64`, or something
else.

```text
error[E0284]: type annotations needed
 --> src/main.rs:3:9
  |
3 |     let pi_float = pi_string.parse().unwrap();
  |         ^^^^^^^^ consider giving `pi_float` a type
```

::: {.flashcard-block .flashcard-block--compiler}
<p class="flashcard-block-label">What the compiler is asking for</p>

The call to `parse` is generic. I need to provide the missing concrete type
either on the function call or on the variable receiving the result.
:::

## Fix it with the turbofish

The `::<f32>` after `parse` gives the compiler the type directly:

```rust
fn main() {
    let pi_string = "3.1415";
    let pi_float = pi_string.parse::<f32>().unwrap();
    println!("{}", pi_float);
}
```

```text
3.1415
```

## Or use a type annotation

The same information can come from the variable:

```rust
fn main() {
    let pi_string = "3.1415";
    let pi_float: f32 = pi_string.parse().unwrap();
    println!("{}", pi_float);
}
```

Both versions compile. I tend to use the form that makes the type easiest to
see where I am reading the code.

::: {.flashcard-block .flashcard-block--remember}
<p class="flashcard-block-label">What I keep in my head</p>

`::<T>` fills in a generic type explicitly. With `parse::<f32>()`, the `f32`
is the concrete type that Rust could not infer on its own.
:::
